title: Visual Scanning and Collision Avoidance
summary: Build a scan that finds small, stationary-looking traffic before the closure rate removes your options.
objectives: Explain the visual limitations that affect traffic detection.
Use clearing procedures matched to aircraft blind spots.
Combine visual scanning, predictable behavior, and traffic services without treating any one as complete protection.

sections.title: Why a continuous glance misses traffic
sections.body:
Sharp daylight detail occupies a small part of the visual field. Sweeping the eyes rapidly across the entire windscreen gives a feeling of coverage without allowing enough time to detect a small aircraft. Scan successive sectors with deliberate pauses, looking above and below the horizon as well as along it. Move the head to see around a windshield post.

The retinal center is cone-rich and suited to daylight detail and color. Rods away from the center are more sensitive in darkness. At night, slightly off-center viewing can reveal a dim target lost when stared at directly. The optic-nerve blind spot is a separate anatomical limitation; it is not the same as the night blind spot.
sections.deep:
Why: detection requires contrast, a useful focus, and enough viewing time. Fatigue, hypoxia, glare, dirty transparencies, haze, and frequent near-to-far refocusing all reduce the margin. In an empty or hazy field, the eyes may relax to an unhelpfully near distance. Deliberately refocus on distant features, then resume the scan. Use suitable eye protection and cockpit lighting without sacrificing the ability to see relevant displays.

FAA scanning guidance suggests short movements no larger than about ten degrees and observing each area for at least a second. Treat that as a technique to practice, not an assurance that a completed scan found everything.

sections.title: The collision target may look stationary
sections.body:
An airplane on a collision course can remain near the same place on your windscreen while its image becomes larger. Little relative angular motion is a warning, not reassurance. An aircraft whose bearing moves may still be a threat if its path or altitude changes. Keep tracking the encounter and create separation early.

Closure combines the motion of both aircraft. Two aircraft approaching head-on at 120 knots each close at 240 knots: four nautical miles per minute. From one nautical mile apart, only 15 seconds remain if both continue unchanged. Detection, recognition, choosing an action, and aircraft response all consume that time.
sections.deep:
Why: in a simple constant-velocity collision geometry, the relative-position vector stays pointed in the same direction while its length shrinks. The target therefore appears almost motionless until late in the encounter, when its angular size grows rapidly. This explains why scanning only for obvious movement is unreliable.

Apply it: describe traffic by position, altitude, movement, and distance, and establish clear control ownership if action is required. Do not allow a student’s search to become a prolonged fixation on one sector. Maintain aircraft control and a broad traffic picture while making the appropriate avoidance maneuver.

sections.title: Clearing is an ongoing process
sections.body:
Clear the intended flight path before turns, climbs, descents, and maneuvers. Aircraft structure changes which areas are hidden: a high wing can hide the inside of a turn or traffic above; a low wing can hide traffic below. Move the aircraft and your head appropriately to reveal those areas while remaining within a safe, planned flight path.

A pair of clearing turns may be a useful local training procedure, but there is no universal rule that exactly two 90-degree turns guarantee a clear practice area. The scan must continue during the maneuver. Verbal calls such as “clear left” should reflect an actual look rather than a memorized response.
sections.deep:
Apply it: before rolling into a left turn in a high-wing trainer, briefly reveal and inspect the area the wing would otherwise cover. During climbs and descents, use appropriate clearing techniques rather than holding a blind attitude indefinitely. Avoid descending into a traffic pattern without checking traffic at the entry altitude.

A clearance from ATC does not prove the runway or approach is physically clear. Scan the approach areas before runway entry and the runway environment before landing. If a threat conflicts with an instruction, maintain safety and promptly advise ATC rather than assuming someone else has already resolved it.

sections.title: Predictability and right of way
sections.body:
Under 91.113, when weather permits, pilots operating under IFR as well as VFR must remain vigilant to see and avoid other aircraft. ATC separation responsibilities vary with airspace and services; receiving a clearance or flight following does not remove the pilot’s visual responsibility.

For a head-on encounter, each aircraft alters course to the right. For converging aircraft of the same category at approximately the same altitude, the aircraft with the other on its right yields. An overtaking aircraft stays clear and passes to the right. Other rules cover category priority, distress, and landing. Right of way is a framework for predictable action, not permission to continue into a collision.
sections.deep:
Why: a shared response convention reduces the chance that two pilots choose conflicting avoidance actions. Predictable pattern entries and published traffic directions similarly reduce uncertainty near an airport. An aircraft at a lower altitude on approach has landing priority subject to the rule’s limitations; it may not exploit that position to cut in front of another aircraft on final or overtake it.

Use the actual regulation and airport publications when teaching exceptions and local procedures. A radio announcement broadcasts an intention. It does not reserve airspace, establish a runway clearance at a non-towered airport, or change an existing right-of-way obligation.

sections.title: Traffic displays, ATC, radios, and lighting
sections.body:
ADS-B In, radar traffic advisories, CTAF calls, aircraft lights, and a second set of eyes can help aim your scan. Each adds information with limits. A display may omit unequipped aircraft, contain delayed reports, or show a target whose altitude or position is uncertain. Absence of a symbol does not establish an empty sky.

ATC clock-position traffic calls generally refer to the aircraft’s observed ground track rather than a measured cockpit heading. A crosswind can therefore shift the expected visual direction. Confirm the traffic call’s altitude, distance, and direction of travel. “Traffic in sight” should identify the correct target, not simply any airplane nearby.
sections.deep:
Why: safety layers are most useful when their failure modes differ. A clean windscreen and a systematic outside scan address visual detection. A radio report helps build a traffic model. A display helps locate an equipped target. Those tools fail differently, so combining them is better than substituting one for all the others.

Ask passengers to report traffic with a simple clock position and relative height. Use lighting appropriate to the aircraft and situation; bright strobes in cloud or near other pilots can impair rather than improve visibility. Synthetic vision depicts modeled terrain and obstacles; it does not make unseen aircraft disappear.

sections.title: Where to expect concentrated risk
sections.body:
Traffic converges near airports, final approaches, common practice areas, navigation fixes, and popular routes. Good visibility can increase the number of aircraft in those areas while making pilots less suspicious of risk. Watch for an aircraft descending onto a high-wing airplane from above or a low-wing aircraft hiding traffic beneath it.

Before a lesson, choose an area, altitude plan, escape direction, and division of scanning responsibility. Keep heads-down programming brief and deliberate. If the area becomes crowded, move or defer a maneuver rather than trying to complete the lesson inside an inadequate margin.
sections.deep:
Teach it: have the student identify likely conflicts from an airport diagram and the planned practice-area route. Then ask what a radio or display would miss. Evaluate how the student resumes a full scan after locating one reported aircraft.

A useful standard is observable behavior: the learner checks aircraft blind spots, keeps flight-path control during a search, reports a specific target accurately, and acts before the encounter becomes urgent. Repeatedly asking “do you see it?” without defining who is flying or which sector to inspect can consume the very attention needed for avoidance.

teachBack: Use a cockpit model to show how a high wing hides traffic during a turn.
Calculate the closure time for two 120-knot aircraft one nautical mile apart, then discuss the time required to react.
Explain why a blank traffic display and a radar advisory are both incomplete evidence.
takeaways: Pause the scan long enough to detect small targets.
A steady bearing with decreasing range is a serious warning.
Clear continuously, including aircraft blind spots.

quiz.question: A small aircraft remains at nearly the same place on the windscreen and grows larger. What does that suggest?
options: A collision course may exist.
The other aircraft must be hovering.
The traffic is safely passing behind.
The target can be ignored because it has no angular motion.
feedback: A nearly constant relative bearing with shrinking range is consistent with collision geometry.
Relative angular position does not determine whether the other aircraft is stationary over the ground.
The observation does not establish a safe passing path.
Lack of angular motion is part of the warning, not evidence of safety.
quiz.hint: Think about the direction and length of the relative-position vector.

quiz.question: Two aircraft fly directly toward each other at 120 knots each. They are one nautical mile apart. Assuming unchanged speeds and paths, how long until their positions coincide?
options: 7.5 seconds.
15 seconds.
30 seconds.
60 seconds.
feedback: At 240 knots the aircraft close four nautical miles per minute, so one mile takes 15 seconds.
Their combined closure speed is 240 knots, equal to four nautical miles per minute; one divided by four minutes is 15 seconds.
Thirty seconds would correspond to only 120 knots of closure.
Sixty seconds would correspond to only 60 knots of closure.
quiz.hint: Add their speeds before converting nautical miles per hour into miles per minute.

quiz.question: Before a maneuver, a student completes the school’s clearing-turn procedure. What should the instructor expect next?
options: The outside scan may stop for the maneuver.
A blank ADS-B display becomes the sole traffic reference.
Clearing and scanning continue throughout the maneuver.
The student must repeat exactly the same turn sequence every ten seconds.
feedback: Traffic can enter the area after an initial clearing procedure.
Displays can omit or delay traffic and do not replace the outside scan.
An initial check establishes only a temporary picture that must be updated.
A fixed arbitrary interval does not address the actual blind spots and traffic geometry.
quiz.hint: A clear area is a changing condition.

quiz.question: Two airplanes of the same category approach nearly head-on at the same altitude. What is the standard right-of-way response?
options: Both turn left.
The faster aircraft maintains course.
Only the aircraft on an IFR flight plan turns.
Each alters course to the right.
feedback: Turning left contradicts the head-on convention in 91.113.
Speed does not give the faster aircraft head-on priority.
Visual avoidance obligations apply under IFR and VFR when weather permits.
A common rightward response reduces the chance of conflicting avoidance choices.
quiz.hint: Use the rule specific to head-on encounters, not convergence or overtaking.

quiz.question: ATC reports traffic at your two o’clock, but a strong crosswind creates a large crab angle. Why might the traffic appear away from your cockpit’s apparent two o’clock?
options: ATC normally uses observed ground track for clock calls.
ATC measures the direction of your nose with radar.
Clock calls describe magnetic bearing from the airport.
Crosswind changes the target’s color on the display.
feedback: The track-based reference can differ from the heading seen over the nose.
Radar tracking generally supplies movement over the ground rather than actual cockpit heading.
A clock call is relative traffic information, not an airport-based magnetic bearing.
Color is not the mechanism causing the visual offset.
quiz.hint: Distinguish where the aircraft points from where it moves.

quiz.question: During a hazy practice-area flight, the student stares far ahead continuously but misses nearby traffic. Which change best improves the scan?
options: Sweep the eyes faster without pausing.
Use deliberate sectors, pauses, distant refocusing, and blind-spot checks.
Look only where traffic symbols are displayed.
Keep both pilots looking inside until the haze improves.
feedback: Rapid sweeping may reduce the time available for detection.
The technique addresses focus, narrow high-acuity vision, and structural blind spots.
Not all aircraft appear on the traffic display.
Removing both outside scans increases exposure while traffic continues moving.
quiz.hint: Improve how the eyes acquire a target rather than merely increasing apparent coverage.
